newsitem.title: UK: UK gilts this week - U.S. data overshadow election.
newsitem.headline: UK gilts this week - U.S. data overshadow election.

text.p: Thursday's British election looks set to take second place to a raft of U.S. data this week as far as the UK gilts market is concerned. With victory by the opposition Labour party widely discounted and no major British economic data due, analysts say U.S. employment costs, GDP and non-farm payrolls numbers are likely to take centre stage.

Futures brokers were complaining on Monday about the absence of the volatility they normally enjoy in the run-up to an election. There was also little evidence of the switching from conventional into index-linked gilts which many had expected.
"The jitters of last week, which centred on the idea that there might be a hung parliament, seem to have disappeared," said Andrew Davies of London Bond Broking.
"Unless there is something very curious in the opinion polls in the last week of the campaign, I wouldn't have thought the market is going to react very much."
Opinion polls point to a clear Labour lead and markets appear convinced that a new government would raise interest rates quickly and tighten fiscal policy within a few months.
"The gilt/Bund spread will probably remain just below 2.0 percent until the election and any hikes in the base rate are over," said Michael Saunders of Salomon Brothers.

"However, once these hurdles have been cleared, lower UK inflation and a cautious policy stance are likely to allow a marked drop in the gilt/Bund spread later this year." The spread narrowed to 187 basis points on Monday from 192 on Friday.
Kevin Adams, gilts analyst at BZW, sees scope for substantial narrowing by the end of the week provided there are no major upsets on the U.S. data front.
"If the U.S. is neutral and the election result as expected, I think we could see the spread down around the low 170s by the end of this week," he said.

The U.S. data calendar gets underway in earnest on Tueday with first quarter employment costs, expected to show an acceleration in the year-on-year rate to around 3.5 percent, and March durable goods orders, expected to remain at record levels.

First quarter GDP data on Wednesday are likely to show continued steady growth, while April non-farm payrolls on Friday are expected to show growth of around 211,000 compared with 175,000 the previous month.

"The U.S. market faces a potentially very testing week," Adams said. "There must be a risk that the data come in on stronger side of expectations. My tendency would be to fear that we could see U.S. yields around 7.20 by the end of the week."
The long bond was yielding 7.14 percent on Monday morning.
Adams said that in the gilts market, activity is likely to remain very thin and nervous until the election.
"If we see a Labour majority of around 100 seats plus, there could be a modest rally in the market -- that could see 10 or 15 basis points off 10-year yields," he said.
But reaction to the election result on Friday could be muted because U.S. payrolls data are due in the early afternoon and the market will be closed on Monday for the May Day holiday.

Traders will also be looking ahead to the next UK monetary meeting on May 7, which, if the polls are right, is likely to be the first official encounter between Bank of England Governor Eddie George and Labour Chancellor Gordon Brown.
Davies believes the market is increasingly anticipating a rise in official interest rates of half a point from the present 6.0 percent rather than a quarter.

"Short sterling is factoring in a rise a little above 3/8," he said. "There are advantages in doing a half at this stage -- it gets Brown off on a strong note and will keep Mr George quiet for a while. Brown can then put interest rates on the back burner while he frames his budget."
Adams of BZW sees gilts in a narrow half-point trading range for most of the week. The June contract was up 10/32 at 109-02 at midday on Monday.

"On the downside, there are a number of very long-term trendlines which are at risk of being broken if the U.S. market went through a rough time. We're probably talking about levels around 108-16, which is not terribly far from where we are."
Adams is surprised at the apparent lack of interest in index-linked gilts, which might have been expected to benefit from pre-election defensive plays.

"Index-linked are reasonably well valued against the conventional market," Adams says. "They are, I would have thought, stunningly good value against the equity market. You drop yield to go out of linkers into equities, which seems an extraordinary situation at this stage of the cycle."
